utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry that we started late this morning, and we may stay here longer to make up the time we lost. But we have to finish this witness today. Ms. Sinatra, you have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do my best to complete it during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Sinatra: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dobro jutro, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to start with a couple of questions that are random. They're not put in any context like I try to do. Just clarify for the record, Mr. Obrenovic: You were not present at any time in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Obrenovic, you -- there could be evidence that you were in the -- in Bratunac on the evening of the 13th of July, between 2000 and 2400 hours; right? Nobody saw you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to. I know where I was on the 13th, in the evening, as I've already said. I was in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. Thereafter, I made two telephone calls, one to the corps command, and then, together with my units, I went to Snagovo, and that's where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Zvornik Brigade have its 9th Battalion at Misici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, we did not have a 9th Battalion in July 1995. The Zvornik Infantry Brigade had ten battalions, ten infantry battalions, but that was up to September 1993. In 1993, this was reduced by -- to six and then to eight, and this was done on the order of the commander. As I said, at that time it did not have a 9th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a 9th Battalion was formed, was Milenko K-a-j-t-a-z [sic], was he the commander of the 9th Battalion? I'm sorry. I don't know how to pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Milenko Kajtez was commander of the battalion in Memici, and if my memory serves me well, because things changed very fast, so when he was in Staro Selo in Memici, when he was the commander of the battalion there, his battalion was the 6th Battalion. Later on he was the commander of -- I don't know whether it was the 7th Battalion, but it was the same battalion that was later on the 4th Battalion in Kitovnica. That was its designation. In July, I believe that Kajtez was the chief of anti-aircraft defence, but he was not in Zvornik, because he was either somewhere else or he was on sick leave. He was not in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was present at Misici [sic] in July of 1995 from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Misici? Nisici. All right. Nisici -- this is a geographical term for the area that is in the zone of the Sarajevo Romanija corps, south of Sarajevo. We had a unit there. It was a company. I don't know who was there. The Zvornik Brigade had locations in five or six positions outside of its area of responsibility. One of those locations was Nisici, and I don't know who was there. You can probably find it in the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your driver that you had with you on July 14th, 1995 was always present with you between 1300 hours and 1400 hours, wasn't he, and his name was Ljubisa Danojlovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Danojlovic. He used to drive me wherever I went. If I didn't have to go anywhere, if I was in the headquarters of the brigade, he would either be there with me, or sometimes, since we didn't have enough vehicles, he would be sent to carry out another task. If I had to go somewhere, it would be Ljubisa who would take me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going into a group of questions regarding the intercepts from his June 4th, 2003 statement, and just for assistance and to make this go quicker, I would ask the usher to please put these pages on the ELMO instead of having the Court trying to find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: -- As we go through. Thank you. And we're providing Mr. Obrenovic a copy of his statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obrenovic, the main communications system was located on the top of Mount Gucevo, which is on the Bosnia-Serbian border, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the radio relay connection, that is correct. Gucevo is on the Serbian side of the mountain, and the station, the radio station, was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to page 85 in the English version of your June 4th, 2003 statement, which is the B/C/S page 62. We discussed our not being able to get custody of any of the VRS intercepts. I believe you testified that you had seen some of the VRS intercepts. On page 85, in the English version, line 31, Mr. McCloskey asks: "Did you have a chance to look at VRS intercepts, either tactical or corps level, after you were aware that there was an investigation?" Answer: "No, I didn't. I couldn't come to that, couldn't reach them." And then Peter McCloskey says: "Were they keeping those records in 1988 through 1999?" Your answer: "So, what was done seriously with the recording, that was in the radio reconnaissance platoons, and they sent those reports to the intelligence departments in the corps. Unfortunately, I couldn't reach that, and I was looking for them myself." Is that what you remember stating to the Prosecutor on June 3rd? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also told you yesterday almost the same thing. I told you that I had seen not the list of those conversations but what was delivered to us through their intelligence organ. These are the things that Captain Vukotic showed me. Some of these things are here in this file. Not the conversations themselves. We could not reach the conversations. But the radio reconnaissance platoon would deliver their data to the corps command. They would extract what was relevant for us, for the Zvornik Brigade, and deliver that to the intelligence men of the Zvornik Brigade. We also received a lot of telegrams, and we were given those telegrams by the Prosecutor. The same refers to the radio reconnaissance platoon from Majevica, who followed the same procedure. I was looking for them, but I didn't find them for the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have in your possession any VRS intercepts, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few telegrams, not transcripts, that I had, I handed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go to page 119 in the English version, and I still am not sure what the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it starts with July 12th, 1640 intercept. It's page 94 in your version. Thank you. And at the bottom, line 31, I believe that you stated -- Mr. McCloskey said: "All right. Let's go to the next conversation, the 12th of July, at 1640 hours." And then, since it's still talking about the 12th, then, I'm going to skip over now to page 122, where you're still talking about the 12th, which would be two pages over from where you are now. Sorry. And you said -- and Peter McCloskey said: "Sorry. Who are you talking to now? Who is X?" And you answered: The duty officer at corps command, our operations officer, Colonel Jokic." And then the next intercept down the page at line 27 goes to: "Okay. Let's go to the next intercept, the 13th. You know that on the 12th --"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't find this. Oh, well -- in this part it says "Colonel Jotic." It's a mistake. At that time I said Colonel Jocic they probably didn't understand me. I don't know why. I did not think at the time that this was so important so I didn't ask for any corrections. It should be Jocic, not Jokic, and here it is spelled Jotic. I don't know why. I noticed this immediately when I started reading this transcript. Jocic, Predrag, he is an old colonel who was an operations man in the corps command. I can't remember his first name exactly. That's why I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that's another mistake in the intercept recordings; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the intercept. When my interview was being recorded, when I was being interviewed by Mr. McCloskey, that may be the origin of this mistake. In the intercept, it says X - I - X Obrenovic, if my memory serves me well, and I remember that I had spoken with Jocic. This is not a mistake in the intercept, but when my interview was being typed from the cassette, I believe that during the interview I mentioned the name of Colonel Jocic. I don't know why there is a "T" here instead of a C." I don't know anybody called Jotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because also you know Mr. Jokic was not duty officer on the 12th; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I never claimed that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Perhaps we could just try to fix the -- what appears to be the mistake in the transcript at this point. It appears from the testimony of Mr. Obrenovic that his B/C/S transcript has a Jotic, J-o-t-i-c. Our English transcript has a Jokic. And as he says, the intercept doesn't have anybody. It's got Mr. X. Just so that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for clearing that up, Mr. Obrenovic and Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to go forward now to page 130 of the -- of your interview from 2003, and it refers to a document marked P125 -- no, 123.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What page is that on in my version?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 102. I'm sorry. And Mr. McCloskey asks you, on line 11 in our version: "So let's go to the 14th at 9.10 hours. Appears to be Major Jokic and Major Milenko Zivanovic. And then I'd like to skip over to the next page, where Mr. McCloskey asks you: "Then Jokic says near the end that the chief of staff, Obrenovic, is coming now. So we'll take some steps immediately." It's your assertion today in court that Mr. Jokic was incorrect, that you were not present at headquarters that day; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go to page 132, which is B/C/S version 104. I don't want to read the whole transcript into the record, but basically, you're describing to the Prosecutor how much traffic there is at the duty officer's headquarters and how it's obvious from this conversation that he's speaking on two phones at one time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, when you say "traffic," you probably mean radio communications. I was talking about how crowded it was on the radio waves. And whenever there is combat or whenever there is something going on there are a lot of messages, a lot of calls, and you can tell by this that Mr. Jokic was indeed speaking on two telephones at the same time, and he -- and those who were listening in to those conversations managed to actually listen and hear what he was saying on -- even on the local line, which cannot be intercepted normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also on -- in this -- the middle of this intercept, they have the wrong name down. Instead of Duric, it's really Ostoja Djuric; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in the Serbian version it says Ostoja was -- is probably a logistics man in the logistics company. That's what it says here. I don't know what you have in the English version. And this refers to Ostoja Djuric, not Duric but Djuric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that mistake. And in the same intercept, they refer to someone named Vojanovic don't they, and it's really Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is probably Ljubo Bojanovic. Maybe the person who was listening in made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this intercept, 125, General Miletic is the same Miletic that you met in Mali Zvornik, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several years later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reference on page 134, which I think is 106/107 in your version, line 30 in ours, that there were big problems "well, with the people, I mean, parcels." You go on and he keeps asking you whether they were guarding the prisoners, and you state that the prisoners he's referring to were probably prisoners taken from the combat front who were being brought back for interrogation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I still haven't found this. You said page 107, didn't you? What page did you mention? What page number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey mentions from the intercept the word "packets" or parcels, on page 106 or 107. I'm not sure which one it is in your version. And you state that I assume he's talking to the -- referring to the Muslim prisoners, but the entire conversation with Mr. Jokic involves the combat activities, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have in mind the same thing, and what I'm seeing on page 106 and 107, this is a conversation between Mr. Jokic and the headquarters on Badem. He spoke with Colonel Beara. While he was waiting to be put through to Colonel Beara, he spoke on his phone to the engineers company. So we're talking about two different conversations. When he's talking about -- with Beara, he's talking about prisoners who were brought by buses. When he's talking to his engineers men, Ostoja, Brka, and the others, then he is describing the combat situation. So in my mind, these are two entirely different things, two entirely different conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to jump forward to your testimony on page 137, involving this same discussion. And Peter McCloskey says: "This packet has done most to ruin us." But this packet you answer saying: I think that he is saying two things, first about the combat and then, which is to say about the prisoners, the parcel which refers to the prisoners." Then I go down to line 28. Mr. McCloskey says: "And then the general says: Okay. Don't talk to me about that. What do you think Jokic was talking about? We've been reporting on the number of people." And then you respond: "Personally, I think that when Jokic was talking about a number of people, that he was referring to the indications that we had about the column. Since there was an order not to report and not to talk." Isn't that what you said in your statement on page 137?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I just repeated the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic testified to that very same thing on direct, and so this is not impeachment, it's not refreshing a recollection. I don't know what it is, but I...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe there is a follow-up question by Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, will you give me like a five-minute warning when I'm getting close to the 30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now I'm going to issue the five-minute warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Well then at this point I'm going to be forced to move forward from the intercept line of questioning, and I want to go directly to:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your transcript of October 2nd, testifying here in court, I'd like to refer to page 2444, and the question was: "Can you describe your professional relationship post-war with Mr. Jokic?" And you went on to talk about some friction between the two of you. There was a problem that cropped up with respect to some explosive device for SFOR, and then at one point Mr. Jokic accused me of perhaps working for SFOR." Now, the truth is, that really isn't correct, is it? That's not what happened during that investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not correct. This altercation, if I can call it like that, happened after our explosive was found at Drinjaca after they arrested this man. I think his name was Cvijetin Micic. And when an investigation was organised about this, they set up some sort of commission to investigate all these events, and this happened in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you're aware that pursuant to annex 1 of the Dayton Peace Agreement, that the VRS was obliged to itemise and reveal for SFOR all of its weapons, ammunition, and military equipment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As commander of the Zvornik Brigade, you ordered that a storage of ammunition not be reported and remain hidden, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it happened. And this requires more detailed explanation. But what I can say is that when, in 1996, I became deputy commander in the Zvornik Brigade, tonnes of weapons and ammunition were hidden from the SFOR, literally tonnes, six tanks, for instance, to illustrate my point. And then in early -- in late 1996 and early 1997, we reported all this. But some 60 kilogrammes, or 80 - I'm not sure exactly how many - remained behind, and Major Jokic reported to me. He told me that this existed. I had forgotten about it. And he suggested that this be taken to Serbia. I knew, however, that if we were discovered, we would be arrested, and that's exactly what happened. So I didn't allow him to take this to Serbia, but ordered him to have this put in a warehouse with Cvijetin Micic, who was the man in charge of the warehouse, and he was dissatisfied, and then I ordered that this be reported and legalised in three or four batches, so that 15 or 20 kilogrammes be reported at any single time. This was not done, however. I went on annual leave and the SFOR discovered the explosive, and that's when this event happened. It's true that this was hidden from SFOR. You're completely right about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was an investigation into your participation in secreting these ammunitions; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an investigation into the entire matter, how it came about, and each individual's responsibility was to be established. And it's through in this context I was also interviewed, as were all the other participants. And I was the then commander. I think this was in early 1998. I can't remember the exact year, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you, as the commander, General Momir Talic from Main Staff signed an order to have you removed as brigade commander, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have an order for me to be removed, but he proposed to the Corps Commander that if I was found to be responsible, in that case I should be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Jokic was interviewed during this investigation also, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. The commission didn't talk to all of us together. They talked to me individually, and they didn't tell me what any of the other participants had told them. They interviewed me, and I assume that they also interviewed Jokic, but they didn't tell me what they talked about with Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You always believed that Mr. Jokic is the one who pointed the finger at you in this investigation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe even before the corps investigation began, we talked, and I was angry with him because the whole matter had come about, because he hadn't obeyed my orders, and that's why this had happened. He did things on his own initiative, and I considered that this entire thing had happened because he hadn't obeyed my orders. I said that some cases should be thrown out, that he should do this himself, and he didn't obey this order of mine. That's why I was angry. And at one point while we were talking about this, Major Jokic said: Well, maybe you're working for SFOR. I was at the centre of the investigation because I was the commander, both the SFOR investigation and their own investigation. You're right about that. So put yourself in my situation. Everybody's investigating you and your subordinates have not obeyed your orders. And then some of those who failed to carry out my orders accused me of working for SFOR. That's what I was trying to explain here. Maybe in the archives that were seized by the OTP, there are maybe some documents about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this investigation, General Andric stepped in and intervened in your behalf, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Jokic asked for a report to General Andric. He asked to be received by him. And General Andric came to the command of the Zvornik Brigade and called Major Jokic. At the time he was actually a lieutenant. And Lieutenant Colonel, as was I. But General Andric asked me to stay, and all three of us were sitting around the table, and he asked that we explain what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, because you said that one of us has to go from the Zvornik Brigade, General Andric had Mr. Jokic transferred to Sokolac, and then to road construction at Sekovici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What actually happened was that when Mr. Jokic told the general his version of events, I told the general something along the lines that I've just said to you, referring to details and particulars that I have not mentioned now, in order to save time. But the gist was the same. And I said: Mr. General, as you can see, the two of us can no longer cooperate. He considers me to be a traitor. So how can I work with him? Find another place either for him or for me. And that's what happened. It's true that perhaps after that General Andric said he would think about it, and then he talked to Jokic again, but not in my presence. And he suggested, because he could not order move [as interpreted], but he suggested that General Jokic be moved to the command of the 5th Corps. But what you're mentioning didn't happened then; it happened before, the road construction, I mean. He was at the road construction Sekovici six months before, or a year before. On paper, he was with us, but in fact he was building something in Sekovici with the engineers, either a road or a barracks; I'm not sure. But before he was moved, he came to see me, and he asked for two months' leave. But this was not according to the rules, so I asked General Andric, and he received approval to use all of his days, and then he was moved. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Jokic's sister worked in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters in record-keeping, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a time, at the beginning. She worked in the Territorial Defence headquarters in Mali Zvornik. But when the war broke out, they came to us, and for a while she worked in our command. Whether it was in the archives or in the staff office dealing with paperwork, I'm not sure. But this lady I think left the command in 1993, perhaps, and she didn't turn up again. I think it may have been in 1994, at the latest, but most probably it was in 1993. I'm sure it's somewhere in the documents. I may be wrong about the year. But after the war, she wasn't with us any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She left for maternity leave and you didn't allow her to come back; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. You have to know that however chaotic things may have appeared - I agree they did appear to be chaotic - there were certain rules in place, and the rules prescribed exactly who could do what. This is the first time I'm hearing that I was able to prevent someone from coming back. If you are employed by someone who can stop you from coming to work. There are courts, there are superior officers, and when she was due back, I wasn't even the brigade commander. I began acting as the deputy commander on the 1st of May, 1996, but the Army of Republika Srpska, when it became professional and when the civilians were employed, this happened only in 1997, when General Milovanovic was the minister. So that's not what actually happened. That's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course there are people that differ on your account, but I would also like to clear up something: You said that in 1992, Mr. Jokic was chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was appointed or whether he was acting or deputy, I don't know, but he was, yes, because I took over my duties from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you replaced him as chief of staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Jokic had much more experience, and he was much more -- he was at the position where he should have been chief of staff, and you were on the fast track of advancement in the VRS army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what things were like in our army. This may not be the best way, but I didn't invent this. It was not my choice that I should be chief of staff. You couldn't come to someone and say: I want to be chief of staff. I may have had such aspirations, but what I'm trying to say that is that at that time, in 1992, who would be appointed chief of staff in the Zvornik Brigade was something that the brigade commander suggested, but he didn't have the last word. Then it was the Corps Commander who nominated someone and it was General Mladic who made the appointment. Why they made this decision, I don't know. I have an opinion about it, but it isn't important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed that Jokic is a very experienced commanding officer, and he's older than me. We performed similar duties, and he's a qualified commanding officer. You're right about that. I'm not more able to do that than he is, nor was I then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Between the two of you after this happened, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for me, no. He may have been hurt by this, but I never showed any hard feelings, and I was very correct. 1992 was almost over, but in 1993/1994/1995, Major Pandurevic, who later became lieutenant colonel, was there, and he was very energetic commanding officer. You couldn't do anything like that under his command. And had I exerted any pressure, he could have applied to Pandurevic or Zivanovic, with whom he was on good terms. Andric, Zivanovic, anyone. This was a small army. And I say again: I didn't have anything against Jokic, either then or now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, you're ten minutes past the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How many questions left have you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If the Court will allow me just to introduce some documents and make -- and verify some items, I could move forward, I believe. I have probably another 30 minutes' worth of questions, but I would -- if the Court won't allow me to ask them, I will just put some things on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think at this stage, you still want to introduce some documents; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It's an article that was written by Mr. Obrenovic in the Drinski magazine, and I had maybe three questions from it, supporting his bias towards Mr. Jokic. And I can just introduce it into evidence, if there are no objections from the Prosecution, and make reference to the page numbers and items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this article is part of Mr. Butler's report and cited and as part of all of that, as well as most of the other military documents that have been discussed. So I would prefer that these documents come in once they're properly given a foundation, as opposed to the Defence just offering them in. But -- and we intend to offer all of Mr. Butler's reports and all these materials. But we're getting into an odd situation where our materials are coming in through the Defence unauthenticated because we haven't gotten to the point where we can authenticate them yet. And that may be confusing. If Your Honours don't mind if there's a D on it or a P on it, it's not a real problem for me, but this is creating an odd situation. I would prefer they come in once they had proper foundations on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was provided by the Prosecution, and if he doesn't think that there's a foundation for it at another time, we still have the right to use it for cross-examination purposes. And if he wanted to introduce it later through Mr. Butler, I would still like the article to be introduced now as D14/ -- 15/3. And I probably have two questions from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may introduce that document and ask your two questions. Then we'll finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djukic, could you please give Mr. Obrenovic a copy in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a copy of the paper issued by the Zvornik infantry Brigade, the commander ordered that such a paper or bulletin be published, and I think it was issued once a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were interviewed by this Drinski magazine, and this reflects your accurate responses -- accurately your responses during the interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave this interview what year? 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but if the paper is from 1994, then it was probably about a fortnight before the paper was published that they interviewed me. So it was probably 10 or 15 days before it was issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was after the year that you replaced Mr. Jokic as chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, I replaced Mr. Jokic on the 1st of December, and if this interview was in 1994, as you say, then it was more than a year later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go to page 5 in the English version? I'm not sure in the B/C/S version, but it's -- the question is: What is your opinion of the contribution of active-duty and reserve senior officers so far in the war? Have they justified their ranks and positions?" Do you see the question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, until -- let me find it. Yes, I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you answer by saying: Not all of them have justified their ranks and positions. By this very act, they have not justified their profession, ranks, or positions. A number of people who remained, fortunately not many, were engaged in something else during the war rather than what they had been educated for and what they have been doing -- should have been doing. They have not justified their ranks either." And in fact, in 1994, that's the way you felt about Dragan Jokic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. As can be seen from the first part here, I was talking about two things. First is active-duty commanding officer and the second is reserve officers. The part that referred to active-duty officers can again be subdivided into two parts. First I say that it's not all right that part of the professional offices did not come back from Serbia, although there was war going on in Bosnia, and the second part is that some of them were engaged in other things. And we all used to say - Jokic also at the time - that many officers managed to get involved in the rear or in communications, in various other jobs that weren't directly in combat. And this doesn't apply to Jokic. Jokic was in a combat unit all the time. Even had he wanted to engage in other things, he wouldn't have had time. So it's absurd to say I was referring to Jokic here. In the Zvornik Brigade, there are some 20 active-duty officers. Half of them were non-commissioned officers. You can count us all on the fingers of one hand. It is evident I wasn't referring to Jokic. If you read this article you can see that no reference to him can be found here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very last paragraph of the article you stated: "This war is very specific, bloody, unusual, and falls outside of any military or tactical pattern." Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995, July, you continued to practice acting outside of the military or tactical pattern, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This -- you're interpreting this in a different way from what I meant to say. What it says here about the military pattern: When I was being questioned by Mr. Karnavas, the front was supposed to be 12 or 15 kilometres long. It was about 40 kilometres long. In the reserve we had just a company of military police. Defence was organised according to a cordon principle and not in depth. That's what I was referring to. You can interpret it any way you like, but I have said exactly what I said in July of 1995 that wasn't according to the rules. If need be, I can repeat that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, because we're not going into questioning on a few areas, I would just like the record to reflect that we want to adopt the OTP's arguments in their motions regarding witness tampering and their responses to Mr. Obrenovic's request for provisional release. So I don't have to ask those questions; we adopt the OTP's arguments. And also, we would like to offer that Mr. Stojanovic and the Defence team here never meant to insinuate or infer that the counsels for Mr. Obrenovic had operated unethically in their duties, and we have high esteem and high regard for them. And I will pass the witness at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any redirect? We could sit until a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have a few questions. It shouldn't take too long. And if we could -- I know it's of interest to have Mr. Obrenovic mark, as clearly as he can, the zone of responsibility for the Zvornik Brigade, and perhaps if he could do that at the break, we might save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object to the use of zone of responsibility. I believe Mr. Obrenovic was quite clear that there was no zone of responsibility for the brigade. There's a zone of operation and there are other such zones. So I would appreciate if we could use the correct terminology. Because that's going to become an issue when Mr. Butler shows up. So I think it has a subliminal effect if we continue to use "zone of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the word "zone of responsibility" was brought up many, many times. I think the Judges themselves have some questions on that. But no matter, we use the terminology of "zone of responsibility" or some other words, there must be a clear line to separate the responsibilities of the two brigades in a military or geographic sense. So in this sense I think it's quite necessary for the witness to draw on a map roughly where is the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could -- we have a new exhibit which is an intercept, number P139. It's from the 15 July at 0818 hours in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, generally speaking, the redirect should be within the scope of the cross-examination. There's no chance to introduce new documents if you want to bring up a new subject here. Because that will give the way for the Defence to cross-examine the witness on that new piece of evidence, which there's no end of this proceedings. If you want to impeach, using this document to impeach the case presented by the Defence, we could consider, but you have to tell us what's the purpose of using that piece of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I fully agree with Your Honour. I do not want to bring up any new subjects. This is an intercept that I believe starts out with the point that -- on the morning of 15 July, that Chief Obrenovic is in the field. This is an issue that was a major issue of Ms. Sinatra, and so this is just a quick intercept showing that he's in the field, in response to theirs, and then off we go to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll see how far we could go. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could put the English on the ELMO, the beginning of it. Re-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just briefly take a look at this intercept.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time, at 15 July, at 0818 hours in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, on the 15th of July, at 0818, it is very hard for me to say where I was at 0818, but I was in the general area of Snagovo. I believe that we were advancing from the crossroads from the villages towards Crni Vrh. We were scouring the terrain and we were engaged in combat with the Muslim forces and their flanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In the middle of that intercept, apparently Zlatar, duty officer, is looking for you, and C says: "Okay. He's up there in the field. He's up there positioning the troops." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said: It's very hard for me to say where I was. I was not positioning the troops. We were engaged in combat. And the first thing I did on that morning was that we -- I deployed the troops and went up to join our troops on Crni Vrh. Yes, you may say that I was positioning my troops, but also we were engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who do you think, if you know, who "C" is in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was the switchboard. It is our switchboard. And it is the person on duty by the switchboard on the second floor, on the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need that any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that when Drago Nikolic spoke to you and informed you of this operation to kill the prisoners, that it's at about that time you decided to support that operation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, did you take responsibility for the Muslim prisoners that were stored and detained in the Zvornik Brigade area, in the schools?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you responsible for their care, their feeding, their medical help?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the chief of staff, or the deputy commander, and I was in command of that part of the Zvornik Brigade unit in Zvornik. The answer to that, in practical terms, is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the commander, you were responsible for the prisoners in your custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may lodge an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They're not in his custody and it's never been established that they were in his custody. I think the gentleman was quite clear that he was informed that prisoners would be brought into his area where he was -- where the -- into Zvornik, or the Zvornik area. As to whether they were his prisoners or they were Beara's prisoners or Popovic's prisoners, that is Main Staff, or corps prisoners, that's an issue that needs to be clarified, and I don't believe that this gentleman at this point is competent to make that assertion. And that's something that was not raised on direct, and so it's going to invite a counter-offensive on my part. So if we're going to allow this questioning, which now we're going into a different area, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to give me leeway to do re-cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond to that? That's the most absurd argument I have ever heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to save time, to save time, maybe the word "custody" has got special meanings. I believe the parties will argue for the meaning of this word for many, many hours. Let's change to another word. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you have acknowledged that those prisoners in those schools were your responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the command sense of the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the command sense, as you've described, how important in operations of the military is the command sense, the commander's responsibility? Is there anything more important than that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't. This is one of the basic principles, the foundation of the army. That's the principle of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we have seen today through a document, or yesterday, the prisoners at the Orahovac school were guarded by soldiers from the Zvornik Brigade military police, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only by them, but they were also involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does Mr. Beara's and Mr. Popovic's involvement in this operation negate your responsibility for these prisoners or take away your responsibility for these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to lay some foundation here. Perhaps if the gentleman was shown the order that was prepared with respect to Krivaja 95, in the order itself it demonstrates -- it shows who is responsible for the prisoners. I understand the gentleman here today wishes to take full credit for killing everybody in the Zvornik area. He's entitled to do that. But now we're getting into some legal issues and I think we need to go to the order itself, because the order designates who is responsible for the prisoners. Laying that foundation then, if Mr. McCloskey wants to get to where he's going, perhaps I won't be objecting. But without that foundational or those predicate questions being answered, I do object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, generally speaking, the redirect examination is based on the questions raised in the cross-examination. I believe those questions were raised during the cross-examinations. So there's no need for him to lay the foundations for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll accept the Court's -- I respectfully disagree in how far those issues were delved into on cross-examination, but I'll accept the Court's response to my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, Mr. Obrenovic, for having to ask you this question again. I know you answered it, but I'm not sure it was heard. Does Mr. Popovic's and Mr. Beara's involvement in this operation take away your responsibility for these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do they in some way share responsibility with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the command sense -- I was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, as a deputy, at the time, so I believe the answer is clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were not commanders, Popovic and Beara, but you were at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was deputy commander. Beara was the chief of security of the Main Staff. Popovic was the chief of security of the Drina Corps. Nikolic was the chief of security in the Zvornik Brigade. These are the duties that these people discharged, and I discharged the duties that I've described, that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the villages of Orahovac and Rocevic, Pilica and Petkovci, were the civilian police responsible for civilian policing duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does their responsibility for civilian policing duties negate or take away the responsibility that you had for the prisoners in those schools while you were deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Drago Nikolic had chosen to store prisoners in schools in Zvornik, would you have still been responsible for those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, yes. I was deputy commander, and I was Drago Nikolic's superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I need to ask a couple of questions based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you should be very strictly within the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Like a laser beam, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The main purpose is to clarify certain points rather than break up a new ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, Your Honour. I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope so. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Further cross-examination by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, Drago Nikolic informed you that the prisoners were on their way; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And based on that, you agreed that Drago Nikolic should be involved in this killing operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And based on that, you ordered your military police to be engaged in actually killing the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At his request, I put at his disposal a group of military policemen. He asked for a whole company. I couldn't provide for that. I gave him Jasikovac and a few police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is beyond the scope. We were talking about command responsibility issues. Now he's going into facts that the -- Mr. Obrenovic has clearly already testified, he's even made up facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I have one last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There shouldn't be any argument between the two counsels in this courtroom. You have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not arguing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, put your question in a very straightforward manner, and we don't need to lay foundations on your questions at this moment, at this stage. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you ordered the military police to be at Drago Nikolic's disposal, you knew that Drago Nikolic, with your approval, would be ordering your military police to participate in the killing of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew. I wasn't actually sure whether they would just be guarding the position or whether they would actually be shooting. I gave them to him, and he could use them any way he wanted to use them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had agreed to this killing operation, you had personally agreed to this killing operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. No response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I'm all through for a while, a long while, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that Mr. McCloskey treaded on anything that has to do with Mr. Jokic in his redirect, so we have know request for recross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's time for a break. We'll break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey. Did the witness draw some marks on that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they got away before we could get him the map, and since it's been a long period, we were hoping we could do it shortly thereafter. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we could ask the witness to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a rather detailed task, and to do it under the lights of everybody watching him. If we could take a break, that might not be so bad, but -- and I apologise. I should have asked him to do it prior to the testimony. I just did not remember everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to remind the Trial Chamber and the witness too, we provided him a copy of the model to mark the rooms, and we've never received that back. It needs to be introduced as an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Does it have a number on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It doesn't yet. When he returns it to us, we'll mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, would you please provide the map to this witness and ask him to draw more or less the rough lines. Because the Judges have some questions concerning this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I can -- I'll get that map over, and if we could just give him five minutes, maybe, to look at it, five or ten minutes. My guess is he could do a pretty good job. I know every minute counts, but he's -- I think he knows this pretty well and he might not want to draw just a rough idea. He can point to it right now and draw it later if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, and I would agree with the Prosecutor here, for a change. I would not want a rough idea, because, as far as -- it's going to be very critical on the issue of whether the Zvornik town is part of his zone of responsibility. That's a critical issue. That's what the suggestion that were being made, in fact, through the redirect. And so -- and he -- and I understand that Mr. Obrenovic said that he had received at some point -- not he personally, but the Zvornik Brigade - some directive from the Drina Corps which expanded, in a sense, the traditional zone of operation of the Zvornik Brigade, and I'm going to need to -- we're going to need to look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, there's no need for you to give some indications to this witness how to draw this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not, Your Honour. That's not the intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.06 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Obrenovic, thank you very much for drawing up the lines on this map. And I would like to ask you: In drawing up these lines, did you do it independently, I mean by yourself, without any instructions from anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I did it according to the best of my memory, according to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The Judges might have some questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Gospodin, Mr. Obrenovic. May I ask you about the units of Zvornik Brigade which participated in the killing operation. From your testimony and the testimony of Momir Nikolic, I understand that military police unit, then engineering unit, and Drina Wolves unit participated in the killing operation. I'm right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, regarding the units of the Zvornik Brigade which participated in the killing, I can tell you that part of the Zvornik Brigade police participated in providing security and guarded the inmates in the school in Orahovac, on the 13th, in the evening, on the 14th, and later on a group remained in the school building in Orahovac on the 15th. I don't know whether any of them participated in the killing of people in Orahovac. I only know that Lieutenant Drago Nikolic personally participated in that killing. As for the school in Pilica, a group of soldiers from the 1st Battalion guarded the inmates there, but did not participate in the killings, as far as I know. It is also true that a few machines of the company, of the Zvornik Brigade, together with people who manned those machines, participated. I personally approved for Milanovic and Mitrovic to go there on the 13th to get involved in that. I am not familiar with the fact that the Drina Wolves participated in the killing. I also know that one of the soldiers from the 4th Battalion of our brigade volunteered to go there. Later on he explained to me -- I was explained by Mr. Ristic that it was soldier Gojko Simic. And this is all I know, Your Honour, about the people who either guarded those people or participated in the killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the details which characterised the participation of engineering unit in the burial and reburial operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding the participation of the engineering unit in the burial immediately after the execution which took place in July, what I learnt immediately was that the two men had left Snagovo. I have just mentioned their names. Only later on, that is, after the 19th, I learned some more details about the participation of heavy machinery in the burials of the bodies. When the excavation was carried out, I learnt that when bodies were being loaded onto lorries from the primary graves, and that is according to Drago Nikolic, two or three men participated in the loading of those bodies. Other machinery and other troops were brought by Colonels Popovic and Beara from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Could you clarify the difference between the commander of engineering company, namely, Dragan Jevtic, and the chief of engineering, Dragan Jokic, in terms of function and hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour. The commander of the engineering company, in July 1995, was Dragan Jevtic. He had all the rights and all the authorities arising from the then prevailing rules. He could command the engineering company. He could issue orders. He could delegate tasks, to put it simply. The chief of engineering at that time, in July 1995, was Major Dragan Jokic. His position in the branch was not a command position. He was more of a professional and advisory body, so to speak. And looking from this perspective, he was not in the position to issue orders or delegate tasks. He could only provide professional advice. However, on the order of Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, preceding this time, because of the complexity of the tasks that had to be carried out by the engineering company, and since the commanders of that company were not experts in the field, the commander ordered the chief of engineering to command the engineering company, which he did at particular moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But who was subordinated to whom? Who was superior: Dragan Jokic or Dragan Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Jokic, in practical terms, on the order of his superior, was superior to Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was Dragan Jokic directly subordinated to you, as chief of staff, or he was subordinated to the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to the establishment, the chief of engineering was directly subordinated to the chief of staff. He was a member of the staff, as the chief of engineering. However, if the commander was to order him to be in direct command of the engineering company for a certain period of time or for a very specific task, then he would be subordinated to the commander, be it Pandurevic or me, as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did Dragan Jokic command the company in the crucial time, crucial period of time, from 4th until 15th July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during that period of time, the engineering company had its commander. It was Dragan Jevtic. On the 13th, in the afternoon, I ordered him to take some 15 soldiers and go to Snagovo, and that's where he was. He returned, I believe, on the 17th, in the afternoon. During that period of time, his duties were discharged by his deputy, Slavko Bogicevic. But as I've said a little while ago, Slavko Bogicevic would certainly have consulted Mr. Jokic on all matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And when and who tasked Dragan Jokic with the burial operation? When Dragan Jokic was aware that he is tasked, that he had to participate and organise the burial operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer, Your Honour, because I was in the field, as I've already told you. So I really wouldn't be in the position to give you a precise answer on that. I can't tell you whether he became aware and when he became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You testified that in extraordinary circumstances, duty officers can issue orders. Could you be more precise on this? Could you tell us examples. And to whom the duty officer can issue orders in such extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this authority is not very wide. When I testified, I believe that I said that a duty officer can act on behalf of the commander and has the right to issue orders, or also he can do that on behalf of the duty operations officer of the Drina Corps. These are assumed possibilities in case the commander or his deputies are not there and the situation calls for an immediate order to be issued. And then he is obliged to inform either one or the other, or both of his superiors, as soon as possible, about such an order having been issued. So he has to inform either his commander or the duty officer in the Drina Corps, depending on whom he replaced at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was this communication between duty officers and commander recorded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you are referring to the intercepts, some of the communication between the duty operations officer and myself, who was discharging those duties on the 14th of July, was recorded. The communication between myself and the radio centre was recorded. The communication between me and Mr. Jokic could not have been recorded because we did not have such technical capabilities at the time. Some of these conversations were recorded, and those were conversations between myself and the radio centre, and also there are some conversations which were recorded between the duty operations officer of the Zvornik Brigade and the duty operations officer of the Drina Corps. I believe that we saw one of those conversations earlier on this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you know if Dragan Jokic issued any order while being duty officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was customary for the duty operations officer to issue some orders. I cannot say anything more specific than that. I can't give you any more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was your relationship with Drago Nikolic at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to our communications by way of radio, or are you referring to our personal relationship?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Both. And not only personal relationship, but also duty relationship.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on any particular friendly terms with him. He was the assistant commander for security. I was the chief of staff. And our relation was similar to the one that I had with Jokic, or any other officers in the command. Later on, there were some tensions, so that when he was to be retired, he said to me that my biggest mistake was that I did not have a good relationship with security officers. We were both appointed to our respective duties, and that was that. We were not friends, if that's what you were referring to. But we also were not hostile towards each other. There was no hostility between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How often did he contact you during the killing operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, only that evening, when he called me, and this was in the evening of the 13th. After that, we didn't see each other or communicate until I returned from the terrain, from the fighting that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My last question: Do you know about any contacts between Drago Nikolic and Momir Nikolic from Bratunac Brigade, security officer from Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I read about this when the Office of the Prosecutor showed me Momir Nikolic's statement, but I didn't know that, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Vassylenko. I have some questions concerning this map. Mr. Obrenovic, would you please show us on the map the separation line between the two areas of the responsibility, that is, between the Bratunac Brigade and the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I can remember, on this part here, the area of responsibility of our brigade started at the front line in the village of Markovici, and then it went to Donji Saparde [phoen]. After that, to the facility called Plek [phoen], and then Gromilica, and then the Kozjak feature. Then to Kuslat. Everything I've listed so far was the boundary between the Zvornik and Birac Brigades. Then there's the Kuslat feature, where our border with the Bratunac Brigade begins, and that was your question. Then it went to the Milovan feature, Drenjak, and this way, to the south of the village of Zelinja, in Zelinjsko Polje. There was an elevation, I've forgotten exactly which one it was, but then it went straight on to the river Drina. So let me repeat: With the Bratunac Brigade, the boundary went Kuslat, Milovan, Drenjak, and south-east along the Zelinjsko Polje plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And where is the headquarters of the 6th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade during that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the headquarters of the 6th Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade was in the village of Pilica, in the old school, in the very centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. And how close was the headquarters from -- yes, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a translation or not, but that -- there's been a mistake in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so. Maybe, Mr. Obrenovic, would you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the command of the 6th Infantry Battalion was in the village of Petkovci, in the old school in the village, in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And how close was the headquarters from the school and the dam?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, between the old school, where the command was, and the new school, the distance was approximately 800 metres, or 1 kilometre, roughly speaking. So let's say a kilometre. And the dam was a bit further away, two or three kilometres, perhaps, from the new school. So all together it was about three kilometres from the headquarters to the dam. But this is a rough estimate. I don't remember this precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In your testimony, you told us that the 10th detachment took part in the killing of the detained prisoners in the school. From whom did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, after these events, in the second half of June - no, July - there were rumours going around. On one occasion I was talking to Nikolic, and he just hinted at it. So, well, I can say I heard it from Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And anybody else who took part in that killing? Do you know, so far as to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to my knowledge, this was this unit from the 10th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the Srebrenica operation. In your testimony, you said plans for the Srebrenica operation began intensively on the 2nd of July, 1995. My question is: Do you know whether there's any meetings for the commanders of those brigade units which would be involved in the operation by the Main Staff of Drina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, Your Honour, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic was at a meeting on the 2nd. I don't remember exactly where the meeting was, but I think it was in the headquarters of the Drina Corps. And he came back in the late afternoon and called us together right away, in order to carry out the preparatory order. As I was absent just before that, I don't know whether they had had any meetings previously. But on the 2nd, I think it was in Vlasenica. Most probably in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean that the specific rules of the various brigades were outlined during that meeting? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't attend that meeting, but, as I have already said, when the commander came back in the early evening, he gave out tasks right away as to what was to be prepared, and he issued orders that our own preparatory order be issued. So I think that over there they were given tasks in this connection, orally, and at the same time the written preparatory order arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you know what specific tasks assigned to your brigade and to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time, Your Honour. Later on I read about this in the various documents that I was shown. And also, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, when things quietened down on the 24th, and later, said something to me about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are they just a military task, or any task, any other tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic said on those days related to military tasks for the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: During your testimony, you said that Zvornik Brigade came into contact with Bratunac Brigade, 4th Battalion, at one stage. And you spoke with the duty officer of the 4th Battalion, Mr. Radika Petrovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't speak personally with Radika Petrovic. He was the commander of that battalion. But I did talk to his duty officer, or someone from the command there, on the morning of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Were you also in contact with other officials, either Mr. Blagojevic or Momir Nikolic, at that point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And on the 12th of July, did you have any contact with Mr. Blagojevic, or any persons from Bratunac Brigade, for updates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th, Your Honour, I didn't have contacts with anyone from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you only got your information from Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received information from the Drina Corps from Mane Djuric, of the MUP. And what my intelligence officer, Captain Vukotic, gathered from our group on Gucevo listening in to radio communications, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could brigades have direct contact, or they have to go through their superior commander structures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible, Your Honour, for brigades to communicate directly, as neighbours in combat, but there was also the possibility of their communicating through the corps. All tasks had to go through the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Dragan Jokic took part in the burial and reburial operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the reburial operations, I have no knowledge about Dragan Jokic participating. I don't know about that. My personal opinion is that he didn't. But as regards the original burials, when I was asked to let those two men go, I checked through the communications line, and they said that the message had come from the operative on duty, and that was him. So it was probably he who gave the order, or rather, asked for those two persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the Orahovac execution, could you clarify it? Who from the Zvornik Brigade took part in the executions? On whose order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I learned, as early as the 15th, when I came to the command of the 4th Battalion in Baljkovica, was that Drago Nikolic participated personally in the shootings, our security officer, that is, as did Gojko Simic of the 4th Battalion, whom we've mentioned. Drago Nikolic asked for volunteers for this. And the shooting started under orders from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You testified that Lazo Ristic, deputy commander of the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, sent eight soldiers to Orahovac to help secure the prisoners in the school. Did he get your approval?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't get my approval, Your Honour. I learned about this through contacts with him by radio on the 14th, after he had done this. And he explained this to me on the 15th, in the afternoon, in the command, when I asked him about it. He explained that he had received a phone call from Orahovac, from Captain Milorad Trbic, who was Drago Nikolic's deputy and who said: Lazo, help us. The Turks are going to break through. He asked him to get together a group of men, seven or eight men, and send them there. And Ristic, as he said, sent seven or eight men to help in securing the prisoners. So in the early evening of the 14th, I learned that Ristic had sent that group, without their being detailed, and on the afternoon of the 15th he explained things to me, as I've just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
