utterances.text: As for the burial of the killed prisoners of war, are there any plans for that? Because it involves a lot of coordinations of various departments and using a lot of heavy machines. I want to ask you whether there was a plan to bury those killed people.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not aware of any plan. What I know is that practically on the 14th, this order was issued in haste. And on the 14th, preparations began. Machines were driven off to the locations where they were to operate and they did that then, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judges' questions? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. And most of these questions are in response to questioning by Judge Vassylenko. Further cross-examination by Ms. Sinatra:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you said that in order for the chief of engineering to participate or issue orders, there had to be -- he had to have permission or an order from his commander, Pandurevic, or at that time it would be you, or the Drina Corps; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified that Commander Pandurevic had signed an order giving him authority to command the engineering company, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, I didn't say that the commander signed an order, but that previously the commander had issued an oral order because the chief of engineers was not qualified and because of what they were doing, or rather, Jokic was not qualified to deal with the engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is no written order or any intercepted conversation that verifies that your commander, Pandurevic, had issued any such order, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or at least I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that you testified that on the 13th, 14th, and 15th of July, no such order had been given to authorise the chief of engineering to command the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 13th and 14th, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did testify that according to the regular chain of command, when Commander Jevtic was absent from the engineering company, that his deputy, Slavko Bogicevic - did I say it correctly - became acting commander of the unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have one second. I can't read my own handwriting, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It happens sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record. I believe the record said that Mr. Jokic was not qualified to deal with the engineers, and I just wanted to make sure that's what the witness said, or whether or not he meant -- or he said Jevtic. These names are close, and it seems to be different than what I've been hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra. You may repeat your question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Oh, did I say that? Okay. I didn't say -- that was his answer that he dealt with. I'm really not quite sure what Mr. McCloskey is talking about, except that Mr. Obrenovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic is a trained engineer, and that's why he is an advisor and part of the chief of staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the most qualified of all of us, as far as the engineers were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just ask him -- the paragraph that I thought might have been a mistake has now disappeared. Did he mean when he said someone was not qualified, did he mean Jevtic or Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I believe Mr. McCloskey has the right to address this when he's able to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think he just passed his turn at this moment. I think this issue is brought up during the answering of this witness to your question. So you may just ask a simple question, whether he said Mr. Jokic or somebody else is qualified to deal with the engineers. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Jevtic an engineer in the civilian sector before he became a reservist?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I surrender, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, it may clear it up if Mr. Jevtic is an engineer, then maybe he meant what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, why not ask a direct question, just direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I wish I had the question in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- were you claiming that Mr. Jokic had or did not have qualifications to deal with the issues in the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, what I said was that Jokic was qualified for engineering matters. The most qualified of all of us who were in the command. And in relation to Mr. Jevtic, who was the leader of the engineers company, and his deputy, Brko, that is, Slavko Bogicevic, and the other commanders there. Mr. Jokic was of course the most qualified. This is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it doesn't mean that Mr. Jevtic was not qualified to handle the engineering company, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jevtic was a private. He had no rank. And he was a civil engineer. Of course, he was better educated than someone who was maybe a mason, but in relation to a commanding officer who had graduated from the academy, like me, his military expertise could not be compared. That's what I meant when I was speaking about Jevtic's qualifications. He was appointed at the proposal of Mr. Jokic, as an engineers man. He selected him, so he probably believed that he met certain elementary requirements, at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what Judge Vassylenko's question was regarding tasking Mr. Jokic for the burial operations on the 14th, but as far as you've testified, the record in this case so far, there has been no evidence that Mr. Jokic was tasked, on the 14th, while he was duty officer, to participate in the burials, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's really improper for this witness to have to try to testify in the evidence of -- that's been presented at this trial. I think there's probably a proper question in there, but that's not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sinatra, would you please look into the transcript to see what kind of question Judge Vassylenko asked to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't go back from here to find it. All I have is on my screen. Actually, these questions are really important, and the issues that Judge Vassylenko has raised regarding Mr. Jokic are of such monumental importance to the case. I wish that we could have -- I'm asking the Court for a five- or ten-minute recess so that I can print the questions out and digest and be able to ask the appropriate questions for my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to save time, I'll ask Judge Vassylenko to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My question was: When and who tasked Mr. Dragan Jokic to organise and participate in burial operation. And then the next question was when Mr. Jokic was aware, became aware that a burial operation will be on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to respond properly, is there some location in the transcript where Mr. Obrenovic had testified that somebody had tasked Mr. Jokic to participate in the burial operation? Because I don't know how to respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to help, Your Honour. I don't believe there's anything in the record about that. I do recall that Mr. Obrenovic did testify about what Mr. Jokic told him had been going on in the brigade while he was away, and that there were some names mentioned. But that's the only evidence that I can recall. And there really hasn't been any evidence yet that Mr. Jokic has made orders or tasked people specifically, if I can save time by there. And I think this witness has been very clear about his knowledge of those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I want to express my appreciation to the Prosecution for helping me clear that up, because I was very confused about this at the moment. So I will go on to what I think might be Judge Vassylenko's next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Judge Vassylenko asked you about whether the duty officer can issue orders, and I'd just like to refer to what was marked as D11/3. And you've seen it, and you have been provided a copy of it again. If you'd like to look at it, it is the internal service organs of the command post, and it is for the work of commands and staffs. It's the rule about what duty officers are authorised to do and not to do. And under internal service organs, number 3, going to number 66 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate it. I'm sorry. I'm at paragraph 66 now, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 66. Do you see it, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure why we have a different set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But does this, the operations duty officer has the following duties: Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the duties of the duty officer are to monitor the course of combat operations and to enter the changes in subordinate and adjacent units, and to charts and staff operation maps? Is that number 1?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next one is to inform the commander or chief of staff about any major changes or orders issued by a superior which require a decision of the commander. Is that number 2?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be familiar with the disposition of elements of the command post, the location of the commander, the chief of staff, and assistants to the commander. Is that number 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 4 is to control and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, there's no disputes about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can I remind you of the answer of this witness. Judge Vassylenko asked that question: You testified in extraordinary circumstances, duty officers can issue orders. Could you be more precise on this? Could you tell us examples, and to whom the duty officer can issue orders in such extraordinary circumstances?" The answer is: "Your Honour, this authority is not very wide. When I testified, I believe that I said a duty officer can act on behalf of the commander and has the right to issue orders, or also he can do that on behalf of the duty operations officer of the Drina Corps. These are assumed possibilities in case the commander or his deputies are not there and the situation calls for an immediate order to be issued. And then he is obliged to inform either one or the other, or both of his superiors, as soon as possible, about such an order having been issued. So he has to inform either his commander or the duty officer in the Drina Corps, depending on whom he replaced at the time."

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I already questioned on that issue, then, and I will not go further into that at the moment. May I just ask lead counsel one question, please? It takes me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I just want to lean over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now it's time for a break. We'll be back at 10 to 1.00. And after the recess, if we have time, I would like to spend about 10 or 15 minutes about the 92 bis witnesses. I believe that the Prosecution proposed some, four or five, 92 bis witnesses. If we have to go into the private session, then we'll do that. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I am prepared to make argument on all of those. We could refer to them by their numbers, but it might expedite matters if we just went into private session and then we can sort of just machine-gun through all of those issues and just be done for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 10 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that at this stage there are a lot of documents that have to be tendered by the parties. Shall I begin from the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first document, P115, is the plea agreement materials. The next would be P116, which is this big map that we now, for the record, should state that Mr. Obrenovic -- that's P116, and we will have -- the marked by Obrenovic version is P116 bis. So we will have another copy of this unmarked, Your Honour, and then the one that Mr. Obrenovic has marked is, as I said. Then the various intercepts and documents and other material, we would just wait until we get our authentication materials together. P132 is a list of the first batch of documents released by the Obrenovic Defence team. And then there's P133, which is the Zvornik Brigade duty officer workbook that we showed the original of, that we would be offering into evidence, though we don't want to offer the original into evidence, just for safety keeping. P134 is the barracks book, and P135 is the war journal, and P137 is the operations duty officer logbook. And P138 was a small map showing the movement of the - sorry - the big map, the big, simple blue map of the movement of the Muslim column. And just to correct the record, the intercept dated 15 July, at 0818 that I talked about this morning should be P140, not P139. And the small map that Mr. Obrenovic marked based on his more precise markings would be P141. And that is all of our material, as we are aware of it, that we're ready for at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. There's one question about the P140 you just mentioned. Are you going to tender that intercept into evidence now or at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We thought we would tender all the intercepts at a later stage, Your Honour. And though on that point, as we're aware, there's a continuing objection. However, it would be very helpful for the Prosecution if we had some sort of a legal basis or grounds for their objection. That way, we would have something to respond to and provide the Court with as we go forward in this process of authenticating the intercepts, both, of course, factually and legally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So at this moment you are not going to tender P140, the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. No intercepts yet. We want to give you all that intercept background information so you can make your decision on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. By and large, I don't have any objections. However, with respect to the one logbook, it indicated -- I believe the Prosecutor said that a copy, as opposed to the original, for safety purposes. Now, I cannot think of a safer place than with the Trial Chamber versus the Prosecution's office, so I don't understand why they get to retain a piece of evidence because for safety purposes. So I'm a little concerned about that. Secondly, with respect to P141, which is the small map that Mr. Obrenovic marked, I did see him mark it, but I don't believe any questions were elicited from Mr. Obrenovic. Maybe I missed that part, but I don't believe it was covered at all in order to get it into evidence. And as far -- and I just briefly want to remark -- make a remark with respect to Mr. McCloskey's remarks concerning intercepts. It is not our burden to point to him what our objections are. It's his burden to lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's absolutely incorrect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he doesn't lay the foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let Mr. Karnavas finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Once he tenders them and offers them, if he doesn't lay a proper foundation, at that point, the burden shifts to us, and then we point out what flaws may exist, and then the Court will make a decision. But for us to telegraph in advance what we think might be the problems before he lays a foundation I think is putting the cart before the horse, if I might put it in that crude fashion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could briefly respond. Mr. President, perhaps Mr. Karnavas misunderstood what I was saying and I know that he knows in his legal tradition there is what is called a motion to suppress evidence, which is done in -- all throughout the States and the federal government, where the -- on legal grounds the defence can bring a motion to clear up issues so you know what you're going to be talking about in court, so you don't have to take the trial time to do it. I'm not suggesting any factual issues or any problems or any strategies they have to undercut the credibility of that material, no. That's something that they're absolutely free to do, of course. But legally, if they have legal grounds, which perhaps they don't and it's just reliable that's fine. If they can state they have no legal grounds, that's fine. But Your Honours may be aware there has been a major case on intercepts that has just come down, I think Brdjanin and Talic. I haven't had a chance to read it carefully, but it appeared to be a well-reasoned opinion. So I don't think we have a real disagreement here. I don't want him to give up his ability to challenge these things. But it would be very helpful to get the legal issues dealt with before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I guess I did misunderstand the Prosecutor, because had there been any legal grounds for me to file a motion to suppress, I would have done that long before we started the trial. So my comment was with respect to foundational purposes. So that's the only thing that I wanted to point out. And as far as all the other - his - the documents that he wishes to tender, we have no objections other than the qualifying points that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I would just like the record to reflect that we support the argument of Mr. Karnavas as far as the intercepts are considered, and it would be best to -- if there is a motion to suppress that needs to be filed, it would be best after the Prosecution has put the intercept witnesses on the stand and we've determined the evidence that they intend to elicit from these witnesses. And then if the Court so wishes and I'm sure on a motion of the Defence we will file our own motion to suppress at the appropriate time. But also, we agree to P115, P116, P116 bis. And I'm not quite sure: Did the Prosecution offer P133 bis and 137 bis? I don't believe they were offered into evidence. We object to that, because they did not elicit any evidence from the witness regarding P133 bis and P137 bis. And as for the remainder --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify: We didn't -- so far everybody is agreeing on everything. No issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. We do object to the admissibility of P132, P133, P134, P135, and P137. We do not object to P138. The reason we object to the ones that I just referred to, Your Honour, is that we are making an oral motion to suppress the documents provided by Mr. Obrenovic, and we're basing that objection upon Article 20(1), Article 21(4)(b) and Rule 89(D) and (E) and Rules 95. Based on the evidence solicited from the witness during his testimony in the last few days, the reliability, the admissibility of the documents that have been in the possession of the witness, who was a co-accused at one time, lacks reliability, cannot be proven that it hasn't been tampered with, and I would just like to refer to my Rule just for a second. Under Rule 95, of course the Court knows that any evidence that there has been cast substantial doubt on its reliability or its admission is antithetical and would be -- would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. I believe because the witness has admitted that he tampered with the evidence, there are missing pages that are most relevant to the case, the chain of custody of the document is very suspect, that we move to suppress all the documents obtained from Mr. Obrenovic after they were in his possession for four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's a misstatement. Mr. Obrenovic never said he tampered with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence speaks for itself. Mr. Obrenovic talked about writing in the logbooks, adding names to documents, and I think that the record will stand on its own. We ask that the Court suppress all of these documents that have been turned over by Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly. I didn't quite understand if she is filing a written motion to that effect. If she is, then I would object. It's untimely. And if -- I just naturally object to her and would contest her version of events and would simply state -- well, as she did. I think the record for the authenticity of this speaks for itself and I think it's well within the purview of your discretion to allow this into evidence. In addition, there's -- Ms. Stewart reminds me that we have another exhibit, P133 bis, that we provided to counsel some time ago, and I believe it would be helpful for the Court, because in this, Mr. Obrenovic was able to specifically put little arrows on the places that he marked for the dates and when he was doing his analysis. And so that because the photocopies don't show up very well and it's very difficult to figure out what little marks he might have done, this particular exhibit will -- should solve that problem and perhaps meet some of the concerns of Ms. Sinatra, and that's P133 bis and P137 bis, which is for one of the other logbooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it is helpful that Mr. Obrenovic has done this. However, I hate to be a stickler. There's no testimony, nothing on the record, that he's done this, and so we need to lay a foundation that these were in fact put on by him. Unless, you know, these little stickers and he pointed them out, so at least that we know. Because I don't want to get in the habit later on down the road that stuff like this comes in and the Trial Chamber will say: Well, Mr. Karnavas. You didn't object last time so why are you objecting this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that one occasion Mr. Obrenovic pointed out clearly that, you know, certain words, especially Mr. Jokic's name, was written by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. But now we have yellow stickies. And this is being tendered as an exhibit. I think just one question would solve the problem. Mr. Obrenovic, did you in fact, you know, put the yellow stickies where you marked? At least so we have a concrete record that he did that and then we can all rest assured. That's all I'm suggesting. I don't have any objections other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe, Mr. McCloskey, you could open that document and ask Mr. Obrenovic the questions on those arrows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could start with 133 bis from the workbook. Further examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, if you could just take a moment to go through that to see if you recognise what that is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that -- do those little yellow marks reflect your work product of identifying for us specifically where you made notations in that notebook, that workbook?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, about 10 or 15 days ago - I don't exactly remember - you and two or three other people, in the presence of my defence lawyers, brought originals to the Detention Unit and gave me Post-it stickers, yellow stickers, gave me time to look at the originals one by one, and wherever I found something written by myself, either in my handwriting, or dates that I put there, I marked by sticking yellow stickers on the originals. These are the copies of what we did at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is the same thing true of the other book, 137 bis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First I made notations in the work book of the duty officer. Then you gave me the logbook of the duty officer. Then you gave me other work books for me to produce and see whether I had put any dates in them. What I have in front of me now are copies of the originals that I marked by yellow stickers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I guess while we're at it: This big map behind, which has now been marked 116 bis, were you able to mark on that your recollection of the border between your brigade and the other brigades?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I remember some of the key points that we used for orientation. I marked those points and then I connected them with dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm showing you this smaller map, which is P141. What did you do with that? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the northern part, I drew this line. And then, on the south-east, I drew this line that I'm showing now. This map that we are looking at here, I tried to transfer the things from this topographic map onto the small map. And this small map, it was very difficult for me to be very precise when I was marking this map. This bigger map, however, was much easier to use and everything was marked much more correctly here on the bigger map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for the record, you were able to take your more precise markings on map 116 bis that you've marked in red, and did your best job to reproduce those on this rougher-scale map, which is 141?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions concerning these three documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe the record is complete now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What is the views from the Jokic Defence concerning P133 bis and P137 bis?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of our objections would be that during the direct testimony of this witness, or the redirect, that the Prosecution never elicited any testimony from him except that he wrote the name in. And now we're being provided with a document which has been prepared just immediately prior to testifying. Because this is not the original document, the Court cannot be properly informed about the change in pen, handwriting colours, and pencil, and all of the other delineations that are within the original document. I don't believe that it can accurately reflect to the Trial Chamber what the documents represent, although this is the -- supposedly Mr. Obrenovic claims that these are his writings, and nothing further -- or his handwriting. Also we feel that the best evidence about the handwriting samples will be the expert witnesses that will come testify about the handwriting, not the testimony of the witness who has had these improperly seized documents in his possession for a number of years and has admittedly altered them. I would like for the Court, if the Court would like to accept this as instructive, not to admit it into evidence until further time, when the handwriting specialists are allowed to come testify. Which also brings to mind the books that Mr. McCloskey has referred to. He wants to keep the original in the possession of the OTP. If he really intends to introduce these into evidence, although we believe they are totally inadmissible, that the originals have to come into the possession of the Trial Chamber and the Registry so that Defence counsel will have the opportunity to have them analysed at a future date too. The originals should be introduced into the record of the Registry at this point. But we still maintain the objections that Mr. Obrenovic's documents should not be allowed in. And this is part and parcel of the Obrenovic documents that he's trying to admit into evidence at this point. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just briefly respond, Your Honour. The little few notations that Mr. Obrenovic has made in the book, as you rightly pointed out, some of them were discussed on direct examination. Those books were certainly here, they were available, the witness was available. Counsel never chose to cross-examine on those points. Counsel has had these two exhibits, 137 bis and 133 bis, since 25 September. It's really not -- should never made an issue of it. And therefore I think she has waived any right to challenge this evidence at this point. And regarding the original documents and keeping them in the possession of the Prosecutor, these materials have always been available to the Defence at any time, and they know that. We've sat with them any number of times and gone over them, and we've made materials available and working with their experts and we'll continue to do that. In fact, the Office of the Prosecutor is in a much better situation to be able to do that than the Registry or the Court. As you're aware, the Court and the Registry really isn't set up to be keeping documents such as this. And when I say safety, I mean we have an evidence room, it has all the indicia of reliability of an evidence room, and this material is helpful in ongoing investigations, and yet it's always available for the Defence if they need it. And while the Registry does keep exhibits from other courtrooms, it is -- it's really not the kind of thing that they're really set up to be able to do. And these days of declining budgets, it's difficult. In fact, we've been going on this trial for months now, and all the documents that we have, the military documents, many of which we have originals for, with inked signatures, and it's common practice in this trial, as in many other trials, to use photocopies, unlike, you know, some of our domestic institutions. But this is the first we've heard of any concern about original documents, and if the concern is their access to them, which is I gather, they know they have access to them. So I would just request that we be able to keep the originals so that we will have the burden of looking after them and keeping them and working with the Defence so that they can use them when need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just have a few more comments to make on that, if I may respond to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I know the OTP doesn't have a declining budget, but the Registry is the best vehicle to maintain these documents. First of all, the Trial Chamber should have the original document available to them to review, because the handwriting is something that is at issue in this case, the colours of the pens and the pencils cannot be differentiated on these copies, and I think it would be best if the Trial Chamber has the opportunity, if they are admitted. First of all, we think they're inadmissible. Second of all, the Prosecutor has alleged that I have not raised any objections, or the Defence, prior to this time, and we only filed an oral motion to suppress right now. The truth is that our oral motion to suppress would have been untimely until Mr. Obrenovic had testified as to the chain of custody of those documents and therefore we could not have filed a motion to suppress in writing before the testimony elicited from Mr. Obrenovic. And I have other issues to talk about, but as far as the admissibility of these two bis documents, I believe that they are derivative of other documents that are inadmissible, they're illegible, bad copies, and it will not be of any use to the Trial Chamber -- or any assistance to the Trial Chamber by looking at these copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the intercept documents, I think the Bench agrees with Ms. Sinatra's view that we'll wait until we have the further information about the reliability of those documents. And later on, this Bench will invite the parties to submit any views concerning the intercept documents on this particular issue. We are not going to decide on whether those documents are admissible or not at this stage. Secondly, as for the custody of the documents, we quite understand that in most of the jurisdictions, the original document should be in the custody of the Registry or Chamber. This is the most common practice in the world. However, in the situation of this Tribunal, and especially in this case, we believe that we have already got the copies of those original documents. If in the future there's any changes or any remarks or pencilling-ins of this document, I believe that the Chamber and the Registrar could compare the two notes to find whether there's any irregularity in those documents. And Mr. McCloskey has already promised that there will be full access by the Defence team to those documents. So we decided that if those original documents are admitted, they will be at the custody of the Prosecution. The third matter is about those Obrenovic documents, so-called Obrenovic documents. We believe that before this trial, the Defence team of Mr. Jokic submitted a motion asking to delay the trial because of the doubts concerning those documents. After several days of debate, first, we believe that all the parties referred to these documents, and its probability has been established. Secondly, we believe those documents are relevant documents to this case. Thirdly, we believe that the Prosecution has initially established the reliability of these documents. So we decided to admit them into the evidence at this stage. As we stated in our decision concerning the admission of the documents, we made it quite clear that if, at a later stage, the Defence team will find new evidence to challenge the admissibility of those documents, they could freely file their motions to suppress these documents from the evidence. There's no doubt about it. So, I believe that the documents submitted by the Prosecution are all admitted. It is so decided. Are there any documents from Mr. Blagojevic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are. I believe we submitted a list, and I'll just go down the list. D42/1, which is the preparatory order of the command of the Zvornik Brigade; D43/1, the -- it's an intercept, BH army command of the 2nd Corps; D44/1, daily combat report of the Bratunac Brigade; D45/1, request for information command of the Bratunac Brigade; D46/1, intelligence report, command of the Zvornik Brigade intelligence organ; D48/1, daily combat report of the Bratunac Brigade; D49/1, interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade; D50/1, interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade; D51/1, rule of the corps of ground forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe that's it. And I've just been informed with respect to D43/1, pursuant to the Court's ruling, we're not introducing at this point in time, Your Honour. So it would be D42, 44, 45, 46, 48, 49, 50, and 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you have to understand, you have a chance to reintroduce those intercepts at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's been no foundation. It's the same problem I have with my documents, and I think we can clean it all up. All these documents are part of the Prosecution's expert case and will be all done at once. Otherwise we have this odd problem of all the military documents coming through the Defence without any real foundation. And if we want to be strict as Mr. Karnavas has taught us recently, I think we should be strict all the way around the board. These are reliable documents, they're good documents, but if we're going to provide for real foundations, we should be consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you object to all those documents into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I have no objections to being strict. As far as that these are the Prosecution documents, I would beg to differ. And I shouldn't have to wait until my defence to start putting on my case. I'm on the offence, even though we are the Defence, while we are in the Prosecution's case, and I'm entitled to use their documents to not only attack their case but also to set up my case and put on my case. So that's exactly what we're doing. Now, it appears, from Mr. McCloskey, that he doesn't have any problems with any of these documents. They come from him. Now, if he is challenging these documents as, for instance, Ms. Sinatra is doing with the intercepts, I would like to hear what the challenge is. If he is not challenging, if there are no grounds, then he should just stipulate, which is the normal practice. So, otherwise we're going to have some -- this trial is going to take a lot longer. And I'm trying to expedite matters, and as you well know, Your Honours, I'm being extremely efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Karnavas's offer to stipulate, and if he will stipulate to all our documents, I'll stipulate to his documents. But then we have to try to get Ms. Sinatra involved in this, and of course this is the reason why people want to shoot lawyers. And I'm as guilty as the rest of us, Your Honour. But I think we can probably solve this problem by stipulation. But I hate to dump it on you, but maybe we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I consulted with my colleague on this particular issue, and we also have to point out that the practice of this Tribunal is different with any national jurisdictions. That is, during the Prosecution's case, the Defence is also allowed to tender the documents. From the interventions by Mr. McCloskey, we understand that they do not object the document to be into the evidence as far as its contents. We just have some problems with the form. So in this case, as I did in the other case, we decided to admit those documents into the evidence as the D documents, and in the future, the Prosecution could also introduce those documents into the evidence. Then we have a P number on those documents. Frankly speaking, to us, there's no difference between the P documents or D documents, because those are all the documents that we based our deliberation on. We never look at whether it's a P document or D document. So we decided we will admit those documents into the evidence, and I hope in the future, when the Prosecution introduces those documents, there's no objections from Defence counsel, because you admitted those documents already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have no objection to them using my documents, which I received from them. So they could -- they don't need to put a P number. They can use the D number. So -- but I totally agree with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do. But before I get to our exhibit list, I have a little clearing up, while we have Mr. Obrenovic here too. When we were using the model of the Zvornik Brigade, we offered Mr. Obrenovic a floor plan. He marked it. I understand from the Prosecutor that they have no objections to this. It has been marked for identification purposes as D14/3. And it's not on our list, but the Prosecutor has told me he has no objections. The problem is: Mr. Obrenovic has just provided this copy to us at the last break. It is only in B/C/S. But if the Court will allow us, with no objections to go ahead and tender it into evidence, we will provide an English translation at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So we have to make copies of it also for everybody. We just received it. But thank you. Now, I have another document that is not on our exhibit list, but I believe that it might be best to go into private session to deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: First of all, you have to guide me on your list. I received this morning, I believe. Some documents are highlighted and some not. What's the difference between the two? Because in the Blagojevic's Defence team's documents, it has a footnote there, so we could understand what does it mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I might. Our footnote is at the end of the document instead of at the beginning. And we used the same format as the Prosecutor used, which means that the ones in grey are the documents that we intend to admit, and the ones in white we shall not admit. But the explanation was at the end of the exhibit list instead of at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you read those numbers for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will go forward. We are withdrawing entering D5/3. I believe the evidence was elicited from the witness. We are offering D6/3, which was an Obrenovic document that was provided way before trial. It's a written itinerary provided to the Prosecutor during his interview in 2000. We are offering for admission D9/3, which is the model of the Zvornik Brigade, and it's my understanding that the Prosecution has no objections to that. D10/3, the brigade rules, definition of chiefs of organs; D11/3, the explanation, the rules regarding duty officers; D12/3, the -- no, Your Honour. We're withdrawing that document, because it is an Obrenovic document that was just provided to us on the 26th of September. D13/3, Zvornik Brigade engineering company. No. We're not offering that one either. Oh, that was provided by -- no. It says OTP on my list. I'm sorry. But I believe it was just provided recently by Mr. Obrenovic. No. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's clear now. D13/3 is the Zvornik Brigade engineering company daily logbook, which was provided by the OTP at an earlier time. D -- oh, okay. D2/3, which is the document from the Republika Srpska, written on behalf of Mr. Obrenovic and provided by the OTP during the testimony of Mr. Ruez; D15/3, which is the article on the Drinski magazine, interview with Mr. Obrenovic; D16/3, interview -- OTP interview with Dragomir Vasic; D17/3, OTP interview with Nada Stojanovic; D18/3, OTP interview with Mico Gavric; D19/3, OTP interview with Nenad Simic; D20/3, OTP interview with Milan Maric; D23/3, rules on utilisation of engineering; and then the photographs of the model. If there's no objections, we'll withdraw that offer of the photographs also. Actually, it may be instructive for the Trial Chamber to have the photographs of the original. So we will offer the photographs of the exterior of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. D26/3, the rules of combat for the engineering company, paragraph 25; D27/3, the OTP interview with Dragan Obrenovic; and D28/3 -- I'm sorry. D27 is the June 2003 interview of -- with Dragan Obrenovic. D28/3, the April 2000 OTP interview with Dragan Obrenovic; D29/3 -- I'm sorry. Oh, yes. The document supporting Nada Stojanovic, it's from the OTP Butler report, it's the military police roster for July 1995. And D30/3, the document that represents the mandate for the civilian protection organisation of each city in the Republika Srpska. And I have another document that I'd like to add to the list. It's a document that's already filed in the records of this case in the last -- it was filed 12 July 2002, but it's filed confidentially, and I really think that we should probably go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. So, Mr. McCloskey, you have no objections to other documents; is that my understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I do, Your Honour. I believe the Court has previously set a policy that just mere interviews statements for cross-examination purposes are not admissible, and I haven't heard any special argument to suggest that that rule should be broken. So I would object to D16 interview of Dragomir Vasic, D17, interview of Nada Stojanovic, D18 interview with Mico Gavric, D19 interview with Nenad Simic, D20 interview with Milan Maric, D27 interview with Dragan Obrenovic, D28 interview with Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course, we believe that these statements are totally admissible. They were used in cross-examination. The two interviews of Mr. Obrenovic should be admitted into evidence to show how he testified, one way one time, and then he totally changed his story and testified another way another time. That was elicited through the witness. He already said that he -- that was then, and then he told a different story after he pled guilty. I'm not aware of any precedent with this Trial Chamber that OTP witness statements are inadmissible. Unless the OTP can prove that these people are coming to testify, then I believe that they are totally admissible, because we have no other evidence with which to support the cross-examination of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, in this aspect, I agree with you that if the witness is going to testify during this Tribunal, their interviews or their statements, principally, will not be admissible. But as for these five interviews, that is, D16 to D20, I believe that during the cross-examination you used them very intensively, and sometimes you read the relevant parts of those interviews. I have to remind you that all the transcript itself is the evidence. That goes without saying. So we believe that all the relevant parts in those interviews has been read out by you and is recorded in the transcript. Do you think there is still a need to admit those documents into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that each one of these documents, although I read portions of them, that there is further evidence within the documents to support the Defence cross-examination of Mr. Obrenovic. I do -- I do wish to introduce them, and now that I know that the policy of the Trial Chamber would be that they're not admissible, next time I would read more into the record than I had read into the record during this cross-examination if I had known that that was the policy of the Trial Chamber. And if that is a policy, maybe I can change it for the next witness. But for Mr. Obrenovic, I was not aware that I had to read into the record from the OTP statements everything that I thought was relevant, and so I re-urge admission of these documents, and perhaps I'll change my presentation of cross-examination in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you had better not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultation with my colleague, we arrived at the following conclusions: As for the new documents introduced by Ms. Sinatra, which is the D31/3, the position of this Bench is that, generally speaking, any decisions, motions, and documents issued by this Bench or by the Appeals Chamber will not be admitted as factual evidence in that case. As for whether it could be introduced through the 92 bis channel is another matter. So we made a decision that the D31/3 is not admitted into the evidence, and if the Defence counsel would like to reintroduce it through the 92 bis documents, you could file your motions on that. As for the D27 and D28, that is, the interview with Dragan Obrenovic, we don't think that I we should admit them into the evidence, because we have the witness here. I think he has been asked questions for several days, almost exhausted the contents in those interviews. As for D16, D17, D18, D19, D20, as I said, that those witnesses are not likely to be called by the OTP or by the Defence in the future proceedings, so these documents are admitted into the evidence. Of course, in the future, if, just in case they came to testify, we could withdraw them from the evidence. We have serious doubts about D15, which is an article in a magazine on the 18th of February, 1994. During the cross-examination, we don't think that article helps us a lot, so this document is not admitted into the evidence. It is so decided. And there's a housekeeping matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So except what I have said, the other documents are admitted into the evidence. There is a housekeeping matter concerning the Nikolic case, that is, the document D14, D15, and D16. The transcript did not reflect whether they are admitted into the evidence or not. Could I ask Mr. McCloskey whether there's any objections on your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have a second to see what those are. Do you recall, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please. D14 is the intelligence support of the armed forces of the JNA. Yes. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do believe that I moved for them to be admitted. When we had Mr. Nikolic on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that we did move -- the Defence moved for their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was my understanding that they had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. But it's not reflected in the transcript. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to make clear, you know, this matter is settled. Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness, for giving your evidence to this Bench, and your testimony ran for several days, and everybody is very tired. And I think I should say that thank you very much to give your evidence. The guard will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the counsel for Mr. Obrenovic could be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have about 20 minutes left in this sitting, so we'll deal with the 92 bis witnesses. Concerning 119, W118, W99 and W105, as well as W101. And as for the adjudicated facts, this Bench is waiting for a ruling from the Appeals Chamber. I believe that sometime next week we'll have that decision. Then we'll be in a better position to deal with that adjudicated facts issue, after October 20th. I hope the parties will be prepared for that, including the agreed facts. Let's come to that 92 bis witnesses. The Prosecution has proposed five witnesses to be included under the Rule 92 bis. The first witness is W119. Since we are in the open session, we could generally discuss it, but if we come to the specific issues which might be dangerous for disclosing his or her identity, we could easily go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think, as Mr. Karnavas has agreed and suggested, private session would be a wise idea, just out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I withdrew D12/3 because I thought that by putting it on the list and submitting it to the Trial Chamber, we would acquiesce to the admissibility of Mr. Obrenovic's documents. But since the Trial Chamber has now moved that the Obrenovic documents are admissible and relevant, we would like to reinstate D12/3, which was a document provided by Mr. Obrenovic on 27 September 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Don't you think that will affect your position in the future?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean, I give you the opportunity to challenge those documents at a later stage. If you show us more evidence or new evidence, you know, we could suppress those documents. So now you ask for this D12 into the evidence, which does not mean that you're implying -- you implied that you give up this opportunity. This is my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I do not want to acquiesce or give up the position that we still believe that Mr. Obrenovic's documents are inadmissible. I guess -- is there a way to offer it in the alternative? Because this is with the witness here. In the alternative, if the Court does find at a later date that the documents are admissible, we would like to offer it, but I don't know that I could offer it at a later date without having had the issue of Mr. Obrenovic here. If the Court will allow me, I will offer the document once this has been finally decided at the end of the defence case, if that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench at this late stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I have been reminded by the court deputy that D5/3 will be under seal. Well, it seems none, so we'll resume on the 20th of October, Monday, in the same courtroom. So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
